lines.text: Making a song together takes instruments, a studio, and weeks.
A.I. music tools serve one person, typing one prompt.
This is CrowdChorus. One room. Many voices. One song.
A host picks a mood and a theme, and opens a room.
Friends join from their phones, by code or Q.R. No accounts. No installs.
Everyone gets the same original line, in the same key.
A pitch guide, a four beat count in, and six seconds to sing.
Nothing joins the mix until you agree.
The host's roster fills in live.
Finalize. Even a double click makes exactly one job.
Brief, cover, backing, and mix, in two seconds.
Here's the reveal.
Three text to speech stand-ins, mixed over the backing.
Music models can't take a crowd's recordings. So we mix them ourselves.
F F mpeg decodes every take. Rust analyzes it, with YIN pitch detection in C.
Each voice is aligned, loudness matched, and bussed through a free verb reverb in C plus plus.
The backing ducks under the chorus, and a test proves every voice changes the mix.
Six languages, one repo, and no network calls between them.
TypeScript runs the room, Python the worker, Ruby the cleanup.
Post gress listen and notify connects them. Events land in Timescale, the engine behind Tiger Data.
Every sponsor tool is a plug in, behind one environment variable.
Gemini writes the lyrics and the brief.
Nah no Banana paints the cover.
Lyria composes the backing.
Nimble finds inspiration.
Snowflake runs analytics.
Sentry catches errors, never audio.
With no keys set, like here, each step runs a labelled local fallback.
Every test suite, plus a three browser Playwright run, is green in CI.
Voices stay private, and are deleted after a day.
Our stretch: signal processing in three languages, and Post gress as a message bus.
CrowdChorus. One room. Many voices. One original song.
Open source. Clone it, and sing.
